name: Grout
seoDesc: Grout: work out width of the area (W) from the length of the area and the total area to be tiled. A free construction calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Give the Grout calculator the length of the area, the total area to be tiled, the length of tile and the width of tile and it returns width of the area (W). It suits a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Grout calculator work?
sections.html:
The Grout calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports width of the area (W) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the length of the area (L), the total area to be tiled, the length of tile (l) and the width of tile (w).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Grout calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Width of the area (W)=total area to be tiled ÷ length of the area (L)
Area covered by a single tile=length of tile (l) × width of tile (w)
Gap width (g)=(1 ÷ 2) × (the square root of ((total area to be tiled × gap depth − grout volume) × (4 × total area to be tiled × gap depth × area covered by a single tile + total area to be tiled × gap depth × (length of tile (l) ^ 2) − 2 × total area to be tiled × gap depth × length of tile (l) × width of tile (w) + total area to be tiled × gap depth × (width of tile (w) ^ 2) − grout volume × (length of tile (l) ^ 2) + 2 × grout volume × length of tile (l) × width of tile (w) − grout volume × (width of tile (w) ^ 2))) − (length of tile (l) + width of tile (w)) × (total area to be tiled × gap depth − grout volume)) ÷ (total area to be tiled × gap depth − grout volume)
Grout density=grout weight ÷ grout volume
Dry material percentage=100 × dry material weight ÷ grout weight
Number of bags needed=rounded up, ((dry material weight ÷ weight per bag))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:

  • Shown in square centimeters, and convertible to any of the 24 units on that chip.
  • Shown in millimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilograms per cubic meter, and convertible to any of the 9 units on that chip.
  • Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Area, opening in square centimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Grout calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length of the area, the total area to be tiled and the length of tile — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Grout calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns width of the area (W), derived from the length of the area, the total area to be tiled and the length of tile. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Grout calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length of the area, the total area to be tiled, the length of tile and the width of tile, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter length of the area (L) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Length of the area (L) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Grout calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
